idiom_name: @Serializable data class envelope + kotlinx.serialization; Ktor HttpRequestData
implementation_notes: A data class with a headers field and a body field is the entire realization, and kotlinx.serialization's @Serializable annotation turns it into a wire format (JSON, Protobuf, CBOR) without a hand-written marshaller, so the envelope stays a value instead of becoming a behaviour-bearing class hierarchy. Where HTTP is the boundary, Ktor's HttpRequestData exposes headers: Headers and body: ByteReadChannel (the raw payload) and ContentNegotiation deserializes the body into a @Serializable type, which is the same header/body split with the framework owning the transport. A hand-written Message class is justified only when header validation or binary framing beyond the serializer's reach is required.
pitfalls: Only properties with backing fields are serialized, so computed properties disappear from the wire; default values are omitted unless @EncodeDefault is used, which changes the header contract between Kotlin peers and other languages.
A polymorphic body needs a sealed hierarchy with @Serializable (or a custom serializer); a plain interface fails at runtime when the deserializer cannot resolve the subtype.
The default Json configuration rejects unknown keys, so a message from a newer producer - adding a header - fails deserialization unless ignoreUnknownKeys is set.
